title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 3: Obra Maestra
primary_topics: Chapter 3 of 'A Centenary of Justice' -- the Prologue CJP wrote for the Court's centenary anthology, the three-volume 'Centenary Reader': Supreme Court Decisions as Literature, as Philosophy, and as History; he calls the trilogy the Court's 'obra maestra'

The Supreme Court's twofold responsibility: (1) the traditional duty to review lower-court 'reversible errors' and settle controversies; and (2) the more sensitive duty to strike down any branch's act done with grave abuse of discretion -- the guardian-of-the-Constitution role

The doctrinal architecture of judicial review: separation of powers, the American supremacy-of-the-Constitution doctrine, the 'political question' limitation and how the 1987 Constitution narrowed it (Avelino v. Cuenco; Santiago v. Guingona)

Decision-writing as craft: the '4 Cs' (correct, complete, clear, concise), against 'extraordinary verbiage,' and the claim that Supreme Court decisions are not mere dispute-settlements but genuine sources of literature, philosophy and history
sub_topics: The Centenary Reader: a three-volume anthology of the most quotable excerpts from the Court's best decisions of the last 100 years, demonstrating that judicial pronouncements are also sources of literature, philosophy and history -- CJP's Prologue dubs them 'obra maestra'
Twofold judicial responsibility (Sec. 1, Art. VIII): first, review of 'reversible errors' and settlement of actual controversies; second, passing upon any branch's grave abuse of discretion

The remedy question: when a branch abuses or exceeds its powers, who corrects it -- the military, police, armed revolution, People Power? The answer the US Supreme Court 'long answered by placing that responsibility upon itself,' voiding an unconstitutional law without express textual authority

The supremacy-of-the-Constitution doctrine 'solidified into a granite doctrine': the SC strikes down transgressions by the Presidency or Congress 'not because it has any superior-inferior relationship with the violator, but because the Constitution must be upheld as truly paramount'

The political-question theory (Tanada v. Cuenco): courts barred from matters left to the people's sovereign capacity or to the full discretion of the political branches -- issues of 'wisdom, not legality'

How the 1987 Constitution narrowed the political question by expressly vesting courts with power to determine grave abuse of discretion, rooted in Avelino v. Cuenco -- where Justice Gregorio Perfecto called 'judicial hands-off policy... a showing of official inferiority complex'

Santiago v. Guingona (1998, per Panganiban): the Court took jurisdiction over the Senate's selection of its minority leader because 'jurisdiction over the subject matter... is determined by the allegations of the complaint or petition'

Decision-writing craft: the '4 Cs' -- correct, complete, clear and concise -- from CJP's PhilJA 'How to Write Decisions' seminars; Nicos Industrial on avoiding 'kilometric decisions' yet not losing substance to brevity ('welcome economy of words'); Francisco v. Permskul on 'pride of authorship' and a 'little style' -- 'a judicial decision does not have to be a bore'

Decisions as literature/philosophy/history: the Estrada v. Desierto succession Decision, Resolution and Separate Opinions cited as exemplars of all three; Morales v. Enrile quoted -- 'when the judgment of history is written... we shall be asked to account... for what visions we have today of our tomorrow'

Acknowledgment of the five editors (retired Justices Abraham F. Sarmiento and Camilo D. Quiason, Alfred A. Yuson, Gemino H. Abad, Asuncion M. Albert), the Philippine Judiciary Foundation (Carolina Griño-Aquino) and 'Legal Write' for producing and donating 1,000 copies
signature_phrases: the Constitution must be upheld as truly paramount
Judicial hands-off policy is, in effect, a showing of official inferiority complex
jurisdiction over the subject matter of a case is determined by the allegations of the complaint or petition
the ideal decision is that which, with welcome economy of words, arrives at the factual findings, reaches the legal conclusion, renders its ruling and, having done so, ends
A judicial decision does not have to be a bore
When the judgment of history is written... we shall be asked to account not only for what we did... but also for what visions we have today of our tomorrow

stances.claim: When a political branch abuses or exceeds its constitutional powers, the corrective is neither the military, the police, armed revolution nor People Power -- it is the Supreme Court, which strikes down the transgression 'not because it has any superior-inferior relationship with the violator, but because the Constitution must be upheld as truly paramount.' Judicial review is the civilized, rule-of-law alternative to force as a means of constitutional correction.
stances.rhetorical_move: judicial-review-as-the-alternative-to-force: framing the Court's corrective power against the explicit foils of military, mob and revolution to establish it as the rule-of-law remedy
stances.confidence: asserted as settled, 'granite' Philippine constitutional doctrine

stances.claim: Supreme Court decisions are not merely dispute-settlements written in 'tortuous lexicon'; they are 'veritable sources of history, philosophy and literature,' and decision-writing is a craft governed by the '4 Cs' (correct, complete, clear, concise). 'A judicial decision does not have to be a bore' -- literary quality and legal rigor are complementary, not opposed.
stances.rhetorical_move: decision-as-literature argument: elevating judicial writing from functional output to a humanistic art, justified by the centenary anthology that showcases it
stances.confidence: asserted as the governing thesis of the Prologue

notable_anecdotes: Perfecto's 'inferiority complex': CJP revives Justice Gregorio Perfecto's bold 1949 concurrence in Avelino v. Cuenco that the 'judicial hands-off policy is, in effect, a showing of official inferiority complex... premised on notions of reality fundamentally wrong' -- a striking psychological framing of judicial restraint delivered 'in those days of judicial restraint.'

The Morales v. Enrile epigraph: the Court's self-consciousness of past, present and future is captured in the line that leaders 'shall be asked to account not only for what we did, not only for what we did not do, but also for what visions we have today of our tomorrow.'

1,000 donated copies: the Philippine Judiciary Foundation (headed by retired Justice Carolina Griño-Aquino) and the 'Legal Write' group produced the three-volume Centenary Reader and donated 1,000 copies to the Court -- the trilogy CJP calls the Court's obra maestra.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 3 of 'A Centenary of Justice' reproduces the Prologue CJP wrote for the Court's centenary anthology, the three-volume 'Centenary Reader' -- Supreme Court Decisions as Literature, as Philosophy, and as History -- which he calls the Court's 'obra maestra.' He frames the Court's twofold responsibility under Article VIII: the traditional duty to review 'reversible errors' and settle controversies, and the 'more sensitive, if sometimes controversial' duty to strike down any branch's act done with grave abuse of discretion. Posing the question of who corrects a branch that abuses its powers -- 'The military? The police? An armed revolution? People Power?' -- he answers that the US Supreme Court 'long answered this question by placing that responsibility upon itself,' a doctrine that in the Philippines 'solidified into a granite doctrine': the Court strikes transgressions by the Presidency or Congress 'not because it has any superior-inferior relationship with the violator, but because the Constitution must be upheld as truly paramount.' He traces the political-question theory (Tanada v. Cuenco -- matters of 'wisdom, not legality') and how the 1987 Constitution narrowed it by expressly vesting grave-abuse review, rooted in Avelino v. Cuenco, where Justice Gregorio Perfecto branded the 'judicial hands-off policy... a showing of official inferiority complex'; and his own Santiago v. Guingona, taking jurisdiction over the Senate's minority-leader selection because 'jurisdiction... is determined by the allegations of the complaint or petition.' Turning to craft, he sets out the '4 Cs' of effective legal writing -- correct, complete, clear and concise -- from his PhilJA seminars, cites Nicos Industrial against 'kilometric decisions' (the ideal decision arrives 'with welcome economy of words... and, having done so, ends') and Francisco v. Permskul on 'pride of authorship' ('a judicial decision does not have to be a bore'). His governing thesis is that Supreme Court decisions are 'veritable sources of history, philosophy and literature' -- the Estrada v. Desierto succession Decision exemplifying all three -- capped by Morales v. Enrile: 'when the judgment of history is written... we shall be asked to account... for what visions we have today of our tomorrow.' He closes by acknowledging the five editors, the Philippine Judiciary Foundation and 'Legal Write,' who produced and donated 1,000 copies of the trilogy.
